To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Doppler method underestimates the velocity of diastolic inflow, that this error is larger for the A than for the E wave, and that the error is minimized by measuring the maximal velocities of E and A without constraint to a fixed line.

Doppler underestimates the velocity of early diastolic inflow by 9% +/- 9%, the error is larger in late diastole, and both errors are minimized by using maximal early and late diastsolic velocities from wherever they may be found.

the Doppler E/A ratio is underestimated by 9. 4% +/- 7. 6% and that this error is caused by a combination of velocity error (9. 4 +/- 8. 6%) and spatial misalignment of E and A velocities (3. 0 +/- 4. 0%).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pitfalls of Doppler evaluation of left ventricular (LV) diastolic function.
pitfalls in Doppler evaluation and the potential for improved Doppler evaluation.
the evaluation of diastole by means of 3-dimensional phase-contrast magnetic resonance imaging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Doppler technique is not a reliable tool to assess LV diastolic function and that it is not recommended to be used for clinical decision making.

Doppler evaluation of left ventricular diastolic function, as it is currently practiced, may be subject to significant errors caused by the spatial offset of early and late diatolic inflows and the angle sensitivity of the Doppler technique.
Doppler measurements underestimate MRI velocities by 8-10% and that the error is larger for the E/A ratio than for the individual E and A values.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
2-dimensional Doppler measurements of diastolic inflow are subject to errors caused by angle dependence and a fixed location for the sample volume.

Doppler measurements underestimate MRI velocities by 8-9% and that the effect of the error on the E/A-ratio is larger and more variable, but the error can be minimized by using the maximal E and A-velocities without constraint to a line.

the Doppler E/A velocity ratio underestimates the true E/A ratio, and this underestimation is more pronounced when the E and A velocities are measured from a single Doppler line than when they are measured separately and independently.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the E/A ratio is not an angle-insensitive parameter.
the Doppler assessment of diasotic function is subject to errors caused by the fixed location of the Doppler sample volume and angle sensitivity.
the E/A ratio is a poor measure of diastolic dysfunction.
